Modernization is a behavior change — the container is the costume
blocks.sub: Waves, strangler steps and retirement gates, measured by what turns off

blocks.x: Modernization is not 'lift and shift' (which moves your problems and adds a bill) or 'rewrite everything' (which never ships). It is wave-based refactoring: containerize, externalize state, adopt managed services where they remove undifferentiated work, and retire VMs on evidence, one workload class at a time.

The discipline mirrors the data domain's strangler pattern: dual-run where risk demands it, diff-driven cutover, and retirement gates that require the workload to prove its reliability posture on the new runtime first.
Below: the failure modes that strand modernization halfway, the reference architecture of the strangler waves, and the console that tracks the estate's retirement honestly.

widgets.title: Modernization waves — click each for scope and unblocked metric

stages.name: Wave 1 — Edge seams
stages.detail: The two modules with divergent change velocity extract first: customer notifications and document generation. Low blast radius, immediate deploy-frequency win, team learns the ratchet mechanics on forgiving ground.

stages.name: Wave 2 — Pricing core
stages.detail: Pricing extracts with its schema owned outright; the anti-corruption layer translates legacy discount codes. Business unblocks dynamic pricing the monolith could not ship.

stages.name: Wave 3 — Customer 360
stages.detail: The tangled data module: state transfer via event stream first, service extraction second. This is the wave the plan reserves the most rehearsal for.

stages.name: Wave 4 — Ledger & audit
stages.detail: The financial core moves last, when extraction mechanics are boring. Immutable event log lands with it — the audit story improves as a side effect.

widgets.note: Waves are sequenced by risk × learning value, not by module size — the edge seams exist to make the ratchet boring before the pricing core needs it.

Retirement is the deliverable
blocks.sub: Strangler waves with exit gates, why modernization is measured by what it turns off

blocks.x: Modernization programs stall halfway because they measure migration counts instead of retirements: a thousand workloads 'moved' and a legacy estate that never shrinks is a cost increase wearing a progress bar. The discipline runs strangler waves, each wave takes a bounded slice, externalizes its state first (sessions, data, queues), routes traffic through the strangler façade with dual-run parity checks, and ends at a retirement gate: the legacy component is switched off when its consumer count reaches zero and the parity evidence holds for the agreed window. The retirement ledger is the headline metric, reviewed monthly, with the legacy estate's shrinkage in workloads and run-rate cost.

Behavior change is the hard wave. Teams must adopt the container platform's golden path, and the path has to be genuinely faster than the old way, one command to scaffold, compliance built in, deployment to production on the path in under a day. Posture proof closes the loop: drift from the golden path reverts automatically with a log entry, so the estate converges instead of diverging.

items: Sessions, data and queues move before compute, the cutover risk lives in state.
Old and new run against the same taps; parity evidence before cutover.
Consumer count zero plus parity window, then the legacy component dies.
The scaffold must beat the old way on speed, or adoption is theater.
Why do most modernization programs stall halfway?

They measure migration counts instead of retirements. The ratchet model tracks VM estate remaining, cost per workload and parity gates per wave, a wave exits only when the legacy slice it replaces is actually retired, not merely wrapped.
Can we modernize without a big-bang cutover?

That is the default: strangler waves move workloads in slices, with dual-run only where risk demands it, each wave priced and gated before traffic moves. A big-bang cutover is a signed deviation, not a plan.
How do you handle the integrations that still call the legacy system?
The integration surface names every consumer of the legacy estate; strangler routes absorb them wave by wave, and the shrinkage of that list is itself a wave exit criterion.
What about stateful workloads that resist containers?
They move on a different rung: state gets a parity gate, backup/restore drills, consistency checks, before the compute above it modernizes. The defaults table names the conditions per state class.
What does the team actually get at the end of a wave?
Retired legacy in the ledger, runbooks and the wave calendar, chaos-drill results per service, and the next wave priced. The inheritance is operating discipline, not a handover document.
